blocks.content: A State Diagram is a UML diagram that shows how an object moves through different states in response to events.
It answers three things:
["What states can this object be in?","What triggers the move from one state to another?","What happens during that move?"]
items: What states can this object be in?
What triggers the move from one state to another?

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800262-aa10f3f9.png
Unlike an activity diagram that tracks steps, a state diagram tracks how the same object behaves differently depending on which state it currently sits in.
1. Benefits of State Diagrams

Some objects are fundamentally defined by the state they are in. A traffic light is red, yellow, or green. A bank account is active, frozen, or closed. A support ticket is open, in progress, resolved, or archived.
For these kinds of objects knowing the states and what moves them around matters far more than knowing the class structure.
Here is why state diagrams are worth knowing well.
1. See an object's entire lifetime in one picture
blocks.text: 1. See an object's entire lifetime in one picture

blocks.content: Some objects behave completely differently depending on where they are in their lifecycle. You can withdraw from an active bank account but not a frozen one. You can reopen a resolved ticket but not an archived one. State diagrams make every valid action visible as an arrow. If there is no arrow for an event in a given state, that event is not allowed there.
2. Expose gaps before they become bugs
blocks.text: 2. Expose gaps before they become bugs

blocks.content: The moment you sit down and draw a state diagram, missing transitions jump out at you. What happens to a support ticket if the assigned agent leaves the company while it is in progress? What if a bank account gets a deposit request while it is being closed? These edge cases hide comfortably in your head until they surface in production. On a diagram a state with no outgoing arrow for a particular event is impossible to miss.
3. Translate directly into code

State diagrams are one of the most implementation-ready diagrams you can draw. States become enum values. Transitions become methods. Guard conditions become if-statements. A state diagram for a support ticket system maps almost line for line into a TicketStatus enum, a transition() method, and the validation logic that controls it.
2. Components of a State Machine Diagram
blocks.text: 2. Components of a State Machine Diagram

blocks.content: Every state diagram is built from the same small set of building blocks. Learn these and you can read or draw any state machine you come across.
1. State
A state is a condition the object sits in for a period of time. It waits there until something happens that pushes it forward. Drawn as a rounded rectangle with the name inside.
A state can also carry three internal activities:
["entry / runs the moment the object arrives in this state","do / keeps running while the object stays in this state","exit / runs the moment the object leaves this state"]
items: entry / runs the moment the object arrives in this state
do / keeps running while the object stays in this state
exit / runs the moment the object leaves this state

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800339-a1c76107.png
States are named with nouns or adjectives Scheduled, InConsultation, Done. Not verbs. A state is something the object is, not something it does.
2. Initial State
Marks where the lifecycle kicks off. A solid filled circle with one arrow pointing to the first real state. Nothing points into it. No event label needed the object simply starts here.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800488-845107be.png
Every state diagram has exactly one initial state.
3. Final State

Marks where the lifecycle ends. A bullseye filled circle inside a larger ring. Not every diagram needs one. A hospital system never truly stops, but a patient appointment eventually reaches Completed or Cancelled and goes no further.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800568-439c46f4.png
An object can reach the final state through multiple paths but the final state itself is always a single termination point.
4. Transition
An arrow from one state to another. It fires the instant an event occurs the object is in the source state, the event lands, and the object is immediately in the target state.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800655-af4b9b0f.png
From Scheduled two things can happen. The doctor confirms appointment moves to Confirmed. The patient cancels it moves to Cancelled. Nothing else is valid from this state.
5. Event
The trigger written on the transition arrow that causes the object to move. Events come in four flavours:

["Signal events something external arrives (patientArrived, paymentReceived)","Call events a method gets invoked (scheduleAppointment(), processPayment())","Time events a timer fires (after 24 hours, after 30 minutes)","Change events a condition flips to true (when waitlist == 0)"]
items: Change events a condition flips to true (when waitlist == 0)

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800825-5daba099.png
Name events clearly using camelCase verbs patientArrived, appointmentCancelled, paymentTimeout. Vague names like update or change leave readers guessing.
6. Guard Condition

A boolean check written in square brackets on a transition. The transition only fires if the event occurs AND the guard is true. Without guards, two arrows leaving the same state for the same event would be impossible to tell apart.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245800914-8ccb2a4b.png
Same event, two outcomes. The guard decides which arrow fires. If a slot is free the appointment is confirmed. If not the patient joins the waitlist.
7. Action
Behavior that executes at the moment of a transition. Written after a / on the arrow.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801000-a265abfc.png
When the patient checks in,notifyDoctor()fires instantly as part of the transition. When the consultation ends,generateBill()runs before the object settles intoDone.
3. Types of States
Not every state is a plain box. UML gives you several specialized state types that handle complex lifecycles without turning the diagram into a mess.
Simple States
A plain named condition with arrows coming in and going out. No internal structure. The majority of states in any diagram are simple states.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801151-eb466084.png
Four simple states, one clear cycle. A hotel room moves from available to reserved to occupied to cleaning and back. No nesting needed.
Composite States
A composite state wraps its own inner lifecycle inside it. The outer state has sub-states that only matter when the object is inside that outer state.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801240-e416f54f.png
A subscription account has an Active state containing Standard and Premium as sub-states. The user can flip between them without ever leaving Active.
But the moment the account gets suspended the entire Active state exits regardless of which sub-state they were in. Outer transitions apply to everything inside.
Self Transitions
A transition where the object leaves a state and immediately re-enters the same one. Entry and exit actions fire, but the state label does not change.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801334-d5289210.png

A document in the Editing state triggers an auto-save every few minutes. The document stays in Editing but saveProgress()fires each time. Self-transitions are common anywhere ongoing activity needs to produce a side effect without moving the object forward.
Choice Pseudo-State

A diamond that evaluates a runtime condition and routes the object to different states based on the result. Used when the destination depends on a value that only exists at the moment the transition fires.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245801421-2b83c71e.png
After evaluation the choice node checks the score and routes to one of three outcomes. No fixed guard on the transition arrow the routing happens dynamically at runtime.
4. How to Draw a State Diagram (Step by Step)
blocks.text: 4. How to Draw a State Diagram (Step by Step)

blocks.content: A repeatable process for modeling any object's lifecycle. We will use a hospital appointment as the running example.
Step 1: Pick the object One object at a time. State diagrams are not system diagrams they zoom into a single thing. Here the object is the Appointment.
Step 2: List every possible state What conditions can an appointment be in across its entire life? Requested, Scheduled, Confirmed, InProgress, Completed, Cancelled, NoShow.

Step 3: Pin down the start and end Where does the lifecycle begin? Requested. Where does it end? Completed, Cancelled, and NoShow are all terminal reaching any one of them means the appointment is done.

Step 4: Map the transitions For every state ask what events can pull the object out of here and where does each one lead? Requested can move to Scheduled when a slot is assigned, or straight to Cancelled if no slots are free. Confirmed moves to InProgress when the patient checks in, or to NoShow if the appointment time passes with no arrival.

Step 5: Layer in guard conditions Are there transitions where the same event leads to different places? Cancelling a Confirmed appointment might mean a full refund if it is more than 24 hours away, or a cancellation fee if it is not. That distinction is a guard condition.

Step 6: Check for gaps Scan every state. Does each one have at least one outgoing transition unless it is terminal? Does each one have at least one incoming transition unless it is the initial state? What happens if a patient tries to cancel an appointment that is already InProgress? If the diagram cannot answer that, there is a gap that needs filling.
